transcript.content: Hello, it’s nice to meet you. What brings you in today?

Nice to meet you too. Um, well, what brings me in is that I keep getting these thoughts. I work in IT management, and I just keep thinking that if I miss one setting... or one access rule, or a warning sign, that someone could get hurt or just lose everything. And even though part of me knows it's irrational, it... it hits me like I'm personally responsible. I just can't seem to move on from it.
When these thoughts come up, do you feel driven to do anything repeatedly—such as checking settings, seeking reassurance, or reviewing things in your mind—to reduce the anxiety?

Yeah, I do. Um, I'll reread deployment plans and audit logs over and over. Even old messages. And it's not just the digital stuff, it's physical things too, like door locks. Sometimes I have to count through the steps in my head until they finally feel... safe. 

It takes up a lot of time. I've actually stayed at the office for hours after everyone else leaves, just going through it all. I have to, because if I try to stop before it feels complete, I just start to panic.
When you reread, check, or count, are you trying to neutralize a specific intrusive thought or fear, or is it more a general worry about many everyday problems?

It's definitely about that specific fear. Um, it's not just general everyday stress. Like I was just saying, when I reread the deployment plans, the audit logs, the old messages, and check the door locks over and over... I'm doing all of that to stop the thought of that specific disaster happening. 

I count through the steps in my head because I need to push that exact fear away until everything finally feels safe. That's why I end up staying at the office for hours after everyone else leaves. If I try to walk away before it feels complete, the panic about that one specific thing going wrong just completely takes over.

final_diagnosis.reason: Recurrent intrusive, distressing fears of causing a specific disaster are accompanied by repetitive checking, rereading, mental counting, and reviewing rituals performed to neutralize the fear. The behaviors are time-consuming, difficult to resist, and cause significant occupational impairment, supporting obsessive-compulsive disorder rather than generalized worry or personality-based perfectionism.

Specific feared consequence rather than generalized worry about many everyday problems

Counts through steps mentally until the situation feels safe
Performs checking and mental rituals to neutralize or prevent the specific feared disaster
Experiences panic and inability to stop when rituals feel incomplete
Stays at the office for hours after others leave to continue checking and reviewing
Unable to move on from the thoughts or leave tasks before they feel complete
Recognizes that at least part of the feared responsibility is irrational
